rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh rejected God's warner and warnings for their desires, meriting punishment; the delay follows an appointed divine plan, and their destruction is drawing near.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh have denied the warner sent by God and the warnings delivered by him and instead followed their own whims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their denial stems neither from doubts nor lack of signs: accepting reward and punishment would require them to give up their desires, so they make lame excuses.
rows.anchor: the only reason for this is that they are slaves to their desires. If they accept reward and punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accounts of earlier peoples teach that nations denying their messengers' warnings were ultimately punished by God.
rows.anchor: They will come to know from these anecdotes that whichever nation denied the warnings of its messenger, was ultimately punished by God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier peoples mistook delayed punishment for proof that their messengers' warnings were baseless, but the warnings came true; waiting to believe until punishment arrives is too late.
rows.anchor: these earlier nations too wrongly concluded that the warnings of their messengers were baseless; yet they finally came true

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier sūrahs recount these peoples, and this sūrah resumes their stories from verse 9; its repeated closing refrain shows that messengers' warnings come true and deniers are punished.
rows.anchor: are coming up in this sūrah too from verse 9 onwards. Readers will see that at the end of every anecdote the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle mā can mean either negation or interrogation; Islahi prefers the interrogative sense for its emphasis and fit with the context.
rows.anchor: the latter usage has more emphasis in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is reassured that he cannot guide such blind people; he should leave them and patiently await their summoning to punishment in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: This is a reassuring directive given to the Prophet (sws) that it is beyond him to guide such blind people. He should ignore them,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb tawallā also carries the sense of waiting.
rows.anchor: So ignore them and wait for the day in which a summoner will summon them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi connects the instruction to wait with the parallel wording in 50:41 about listening for the crier.
rows.anchor: and listen for the day when the crier will call from a place near, (50:41)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase points to Judgment Day's terrors, left vague to heighten their intensity.
rows.anchor: the horrors of the Day of Judgment. In order to express the intensity of these horrors, a vague style is adopted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People now disregard calls to prepare for that day, but soon its caller will summon them into its horrors and all will rush in fear and obedience.
rows.anchor: today they are disregarding the calls given to them to prepare for that day, but soon the time will come when a caller will call them to its horrors

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the caller summons them, people emerge from their graves like scattered locusts, eyes downcast and hastening toward him; the disbelievers call it a ruthless day.
rows.anchor: because of humiliation downcast will be their eyes and they will be swiftly running towards the caller.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words for being downcast and hastening are accusatives of state (ḥāl).
rows.anchor: are accusatives of state ( hāl).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression muntashir portrays people emerging from their graves after the trumpet is blown.
rows.anchor: portrays the emerging of people from the grave after the trumpet is blown.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scattered emergence is likened to moths streaming out in a storm at the start of a rainy-season evening; locusts and the people rising from graves resemble this sight.
rows.anchor: One may have seen moths emerging in the rainy season at the onset of the evening. It is as if a storm of moths has appeared.

none: Surah title and copyright notice only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the Prophet's wives may act from mutual trust and goodwill, their exemplary status makes them especially accountable to God's limits; higher status entails greater accountability.
rows.anchor: they too, are to become an example for all women of the ummah, they are more responsible than others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage moves from correcting the Prophet and his wives to urging all Muslims to guard their families against the Hereafter's punishment.
rows.anchor: After checking the Prophet (sws) and his wives, general Muslims are urged to continually check and restrain their near ones

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims must continually check and restrain their close family members to save themselves from punishment in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: continually check and restrain their near ones in order to save themselves from the punishment of the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell's guardian angels are strict and stern and will show no lenience.
rows.anchor: the angels who guard Hell are strict and stern. They shall show no lenience to any one.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Judgment Day excuses will not be accepted; each person faces only what they deserve, and no one is punished beyond their deeds.
rows.anchor: On the Day of Judgement, no excuse of a person will be acceptable, for he shall be facing only what he deserves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only people whose sincere repentance qualifies them for God's blessings will triumph on that Day.
rows.anchor: Only those people will triumph on that Day whose pure repentance makes them eligible for the Almighty’s blessings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet and his Companions will succeed, with God perfecting their light to guide them to Paradise.
rows.anchor: It will be a Day of success for the Prophet (sws) and his Companions. The Almighty shall perfect their light which shall lead them to Paradise.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everyone else will be doomed forever.
rows.anchor: Everyone else shall be doomed forever.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is emphatically told to sternly call disbelievers and hypocrites to change their conduct lest they end in Hell, the worst abode.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) has been emphatically directed to sternly tell the disbelievers and the hypocrites to change their attitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrasting examples of Noah's and Lot's wives, Pharaoh's wife, and Mary show that a person's own faith and deeds determine their Hereafter, regardless of their spouse.
rows.anchor: The purpose is to prove that only a person’s faith and deeds will be of any benefit to him in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without faith and good deeds, being married to the great prophets Noah or Lot brings no benefit in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: even being the wife of such great prophets as Noah (sws) and Lot (sws) will be of no benefit to these women in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A woman can merit the highest Hereafter reward through faith and deeds even when married to a rebellious man such as Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: a woman can deserve the highest reward in the Hereafter even though she may be the wife of a person as rebellious as the Pharaoh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Muddaththir is the counterpart of the preceding al-Muzzammil; their central themes are essentially the same and their names share a meaning.
rows.anchor: There is no essential difference between the central themes of both sūrahs .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Muzzammil prepares the Prophet to bear a weighty message, while al-Muddaththir explains that burden as warning people about the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: explicitly explains what is meant by bearing this burden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet must take up the warning mission and hold firmly to his position despite violent opposition, leaving the outcome to God.
rows.anchor: should strongly adhere to his stance even if people violently oppose him. He should leave the matter to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's duty is to remind people through the Qur'an, not to make them accept it; only those worthy under God's law and practice accept, while the rest remain indifferent.
rows.anchor: He is not responsible for making them accept it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–10 direct the Prophet to prepare for warning about the Hereafter, exalt God, purify himself from what tarnishes the heart and from polytheism, and persevere; God will spread Islam's call.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is directed to discharge his mission of warning people about the Hereafter with full preparation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 11–17 warn that Judgment Day will be severe for disbelievers who presume their wealth and rank will bring them still more.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) should well inform the people about the afflictions of the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrogant man began life alone, without wealth or status, when God created him in his mother's womb.
rows.anchor: they were totally alone in this world; they neither had wealth nor status at that time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God later bestowed wealth and status, but instead of gratitude the man became conceited and vain.
rows.anchor: conceit and vanity overcame them and they held that whatever they had was their right by birth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man treats his possessions as an inherited entitlement and expects God to grant him even more.
rows.anchor: they held that whatever they had was their right by birth and they would be blessed with even more

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers have no basis for rejecting Judgment Day; their excuses arise from worldly attachment against conscience and indifference to the certain Hereafter.
rows.anchor: no basis for this denial. Whatever baseless excuses they are offering originate from their love of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some faces will be bright, awaiting their Lord's favor, while others will be gloomy in expectation of a crushing calamity.
rows.anchor: many faces will be fresh expecting the blessing of their Lord, and many faces will be gloomy thinking that a back-breaking calamity is about to befall them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one escapes: all must undergo death's agony and, helplessly, begin the journey toward their Lord.
rows.anchor: face the agony of death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unfortunate person neither gives in God's way nor prays to Him.
rows.anchor: Unfortunate is he who neither spent in the way of God nor prayed to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When reminded of these duties, he responds with arrogance and walks away conceitedly to his family.
rows.anchor: he would be reminded of these duties, he would express utter arrogance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can re-create the dead, having first made man from a sperm drop, perfected him, and granted him various abilities.
rows.anchor: it was the Almighty Who created him from a drop of sperm and perfected him and blessed him with various abilities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A negation particle before the oath does not cancel the oath; it immediately refutes the addressee's assumption, which the oath is meant to rebut.
rows.anchor: When a particle of negation occurs before an oath

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The speaker's emphatic 'No! By God!' rejects the notion before stating the truth, conveying that it is so baseless that the speaker expresses disgust first.
rows.anchor: he refutes it and in fact finds it necessary to express his disgust before the oath.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says this immediate-refutation oath style occurs abundantly in Arabic and also in most other languages, and that he has explained it at other places.
rows.anchor: Examples of such a style not only abound in Arabic, they exist in most other languages as well.

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some people consider the negation particle superfluous; Islahi signals that this view conflicts with Arabic linguistic principles.
rows.anchor: Some people have regarded the

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Others link the preceding negation particle directly to the verb; Islahi signals that this account too conflicts with Arabic linguistic principles.
rows.anchor: some regard it to directly relate to the verb it precedes.
